claim: In eukaryotes, the SRP Alu domain arrests translation elongation of membrane proteins until targeting is complete.
source: In eukaryotes, the SRP Alu domain arrests translation elongation of membrane proteins until targeting is complete.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: The Alu domain is lacking in most eubacteria.
source: Curiously, however, the Alu domain is lacking in most eubacteria.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Shine-Dalgarno-like elements trigger elongation pauses at strategic positions during the early stages of translation in E. coli membrane proteins.
source: The underlying mechanism is likely programmed into the coding sequence, where Shine–Dalgarno-like elements trigger elongation pauses at strategic positions during the early stages of translation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on genome-wide ribosome profiling data analysis.

claim: Slow translation during targeting improves membrane protein production fidelity.
source: We provide experimental evidence that slow translation during targeting and improves membrane protein production fidelity, as it correlates with better folding of overexpressed membrane proteins.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the GFP-folding assay.

claim: Membrane proteins are enriched with programmed pauses between codons 16 and 60.
source: The results show that membrane proteins are enriched with pauses between codons 16 and 60, after which they level-down to values similar to cytosolic proteins (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A with statistical analysis of ribosome profiling data.

claim: 69% of membrane proteins have at least one programmed pause position in the codon range 16-60.
source: Indeed, over the entire range of codons from position 16 to 60, we find that 69% of membrane proteins have at least one programmed pause position, significantly higher compared to cytosolic (50%, p = 1.5 × 10−7) and periplasmic proteins (41%, p = 6 × 10−8, Z-test for 2 proportions) (Figure 1A, inset).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 1A inset.

claim: A peak of high pause frequency occurs just before the start of TM2 in membrane proteins.
source: Indeed, we found a peak of high pause frequency just before the start of TM2 (Figure 2C) (p = 3 × 10−6, 2-sample t test), extending from five codons before TM2 to the second codon of the TM.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C with statistical significance.

claim: The pause peak before TM2 is sharper in proteins with intracellular N-termini.
source: Curiously, the peak is much sharper when considering only proteins with intracellular N-termini (Figure 2D) (p = 4 × 10−9, 2-sample t test), in which TM2 occurs in 'Type-I topology' (the N-terminus of TM2 is extracellular), suggesting that proteins with extracellular N-termini do not pause before TM2.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D with statistical analysis.

claim: Pauses occur approximately 35 ± 13 codons after the beginning of the first TM.
source: The pauses occur 35 ± 13 codons after the beginning of the first TM.
evidence: This is calculated from the data analysis.

claim: The ribosome exit tunnel admits approximately 28 amino acids of the extended polypeptide.
source: Given that the exit tunnel of the ribosome admits ∼28 amino acids of the extended polypeptide (Bornemann et al., 2008), pausing of the ribosome at these positions means that in most proteins the first TM has partially emerged out of the ribosome during pausing.
evidence: This is cited from Bornemann et al., 2008.

claim: Only approximately 25% of membrane proteins have identifiable pauses at codons -5 to +1 relative to TM2 start.
source: Interestingly, only ∼25% of membrane proteins (59 out of 237) have identifiable pauses at codons −5 to +1 relative to TM2 start, and indeed only these proteins display high local ribosome density in this region (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on analysis of ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The pause duration before TM2 is approximately 1.5 seconds.
source: The quantitative difference in density between proteins with and without pause in Figure 2E suggests that the pause duration is approximately 1.5 s (roughly the time it takes to translate 28 codons, see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is calculated from the ribosome density differences shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The SD motif is necessary to generate the observed pauses before TM2.
source: The results show that upon SD exclusion, the slow-down in this region was nearly abolished (Figure 2F) suggesting that the SD motif is necessary to generate the observed pauses.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2F where SD-like elements were excluded from analysis.

claim: Proteins with pause before TM2 had higher expression on average compared to proteins without pause.
source: First, proteins with pause had higher expression on an average (p = 0.004, two sample t test) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A with statistical analysis.

claim: TM1 in proteins with pause is less hydrophobic compared to proteins without identifiable pauses.
source: Secondly, we find that TM1 in proteins with pause is less hydrophobic compared to proteins without identifiable pauses, suggesting that proteins with pause may have compromised affinity for SRP (Lee and Bernstein, 2001), (p = 0.006, two sample t test) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B with statistical analysis and citation.

claim: First loops between TM1 and TM2 are enriched for long lengths of ≥60 residues.
source: Indeed, our analysis revealed that first loops (i.e., those between TM1 and TM2) are enriched for long lengths of ≥60 residues and depleted of short lengths of ≤10 residues (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) (p = 6 × 10−10 and p = 3 × 10−3 respectively, hypergeometric test).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A with statistical analysis.

claim: Proteins having long first loops (≥60 residues) almost never had pauses before TM2 compared to proteins with shorter loops.
source: Indeed, we found that proteins having long first loops (≥60 residues, 34 proteins) almost never had pauses before TM2 compared to proteins with shorter loops (Figure 3B) (p = 0.01, hypergeometric test).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B with statistical analysis.

claim: Programmed pauses are enriched in membrane proteins compared to cytosolic proteins in codons 16-36.
source: Programmed pauses were enriched in membrane proteins compared to cytosolic proteins (p = 4 × 10−8, Z-test for two proportions) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A with statistical analysis.

claim: Local ribosome densities in membrane proteins mRNAs in codons 16-36 were significantly higher than those of cytosolic proteins.
source: Consequently, local ribosome densities in membrane proteins mRNAs were significantly higher than those of cytosolic proteins (p = 1 × 10−36, 2-sample t test) (Figure 4C), suggesting slower translation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C with statistical analysis.

claim: Translation in codons 16-36 is slowed by approximately 0.6 seconds in membrane proteins compared to cytosolic proteins.
source: A mean difference of 0.56 density units per codon (Figure 4C) over a range of 21 codons indicates that translation is slowed by ∼0.6 s (the time required to translate 12 codons, see 'Materials and methods') compared to the average cytosolic protein.
evidence: This is calculated from the density differences shown in Figure 4C.

claim: E. coli's SRP can efficiently target ribosome-nascent-chain complexes to the membrane before the nascent peptide emerges from the exit tunnel.
source: However, recent studies showed that E. coli's SRP can efficiently target such ribosome-nascent-chain complexes to the membrane (Bornemann et al., 2008; Holtkamp et al., 2012) and that this is done regardless of the class of translated proteins (cytosolic/membrane/periplasmic).
evidence: This is cited from Bornemann et al., 2008 and Holtkamp et al., 2012.

claim: Membrane proteins with at least 80 residues before TM1 did not show elevated pause frequency at codons 16-36.
source: Indeed, unlike other membrane proteins, proteins with at least 80 residues before TM1 (n = 16) did not show an elevated pause frequency at codons 16–36 (p = 0.01, Z-test for two proportions), nor did they show elevated ribosome density (p = 0.013, one-tailed two-sample t test) (Figure 4B,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B,D with statistical analysis.

claim: Genes with slower translation at codons 16-36 and before TM2 showed a 95% elevation in expression of the folded protein form compared with genes having fast translation.
source: Remarkably, genes with slower translation at these codons showed a 95% elevation in expression of the folded protein form, compared with genes having fast translation (p = 3 × 10−4, two-sample t test) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B with statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Translation speed during targeting does not affect the expression of the unfolded/aggregated form of the proteins.
source: This difference was not observed for expression of the unfolded/aggregated form of the proteins (Figure 5C), suggesting that translation speed during targeting specifically influences the extent of correct folding rather than affecting the overall expression level.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The percentage of unfolded protein was significantly correlated with the total level of the protein.
source: The percentage of unfolded protein was significantly correlated with the total level of the protein (folded + unfolded) (Spearman's r = 0.65, p = 6 × 10−12, Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D with statistical analysis.

claim: Engineered SD-like motifs in ygdD and brnQ genes improved membrane protein folding.
source: Indeed, upon overexpressing the wild-type and mutant genes, we observed that the two mutants with robust increase in SD motifs folded better (Figure 6B,C, YgdD and BrnQ), whereas the third gene showed no difference (Figure 6B,C, YbjJ).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B,C with experimental data.

claim: SD-like motifs improve membrane protein folding and prevent aggregation, likely by slowing-down translation.
source: Thus, SD-like motifs improve membrane protein folding and prevent aggregation, likely by slowing-down translation.
evidence: This is concluded from the mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: In B. subtilis, pauses in membrane proteins occur around codons 45-85, with a peak at codon 64.
source: Figure 7A,B show that in both B. subtilis and E. coli, pauses were enriched in membrane proteins compared to cytosolic proteins; however, the precise positioning at which the pauses occurred was different. While in E. coli the enrichment occurred around codons 15–65, in B. subtilis it occurred only downstream around codons 45–85, with a peak at codon 64.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A,B comparing E. coli and B. subtilis.

claim: B. subtilis shows a high elevation of pause events roughly 45-65 codons after synthesis of the first residue of TM1.
source: This analysis showed a high elevation of pause events that occurred roughly in 45–65 codons after synthesis of the first residue of TM1 (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: In B. subtilis, ribosome density 45-65 codons downstream to TM1 was significantly elevated compared to other positions in SD-depleted data.
source: The results show that ribosome density 45–65 codons downstream to TM1 was significantly elevated compared to other positions (Figure 7E), suggesting that B. subtilis utilizes a pause strategy that is independent of the SD-like sequences, possibly involving the SRP Alu domain.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7E using SD-depleted data.

claim: The trend of elevated ribosome density 45-65 codons downstream to TM1 was not observed in E. coli in SD-depleted data.
source: This trend was not observed in E. coli (Figure 7E), suggesting that in the absence of SD-like sequences, the ability of the E. coli SRP to arrest elongation is low, if any.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7E comparing E. coli and B. subtilis.

claim: B. subtilis employs the eukaryotic-like strategy for slowing the elongation of translated membrane proteins.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that B. subtilis employs the eukaryotic-like strategy for slowing the elongation of translated membrane proteins, and consequently does not utilize SD-mediated pauses to this end.
evidence: This is concluded from the analysis of B. subtilis ribosome profiling data.

claim: Membrane proteins constitute roughly 25% of the proteomes in all living organisms.
source: Membrane proteins constitute roughly 25% of the proteomes in all living organisms (Wallin and von Heijne, 1998) and their hydrophobic nature necessitates co-translational insertion.
evidence: This is cited from Wallin and von Heijne, 1998.

claim: The ubiquitous SRP system is responsible for the timely delivery of ribosomes translating membrane proteins to membrane translocons.
source: The ubiquitous SRP system is responsible for the timely delivery of ribosomes translating membrane proteins to membrane translocons.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Gram-positive bacteria typically possess an Alu domain and Gram-negatives, such as E. coli, are typically devoid of it.
source: Puzzlingly, however, the bacterial world displays a dichotomy in the structure of the SRP, wherein Gram-positive bacteria typically possess an Alu domain and Gram-negatives, such as E. coli, are typically devoid of it (Regalia et al., 2002).
evidence: This is cited from Regalia et al., 2002.

claim: In vitro translation studies suggested that the Escherichia coli SRP cannot arrest translation.
source: Accordingly, in vitro translation studies suggested that the Escherichia coli SRP cannot arrest translation (Raine et al., 2003).
evidence: This is cited from Raine et al., 2003.

claim: Many if not most of the pause sites in E. coli are mediated by internal Shine-Dalgarno-like elements.
source: A notable example is found in E. coli, where many if not most of the pause sites are mediated by internal Shine–Dalgarno-like elements, which are capable of transiently binding to the ribosome as it translates the mRNA (Li et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Li et al., 2012.

claim: The eukaryotic SRP arrests the elongation upon binding to ribosome-nascent chain complexes through the SRP Alu domain that binds to the elongation factor binding site.
source: The arrest is mediated through the SRP Alu domain that binds to the elongation factor binding site (Halic et al., 2004) and is kept until the ribosome arrives at the translocon, causing the SRP dissociation.
evidence: This is cited from Halic et al., 2004.

claim: Ribosome profiling enables the estimation of elongation rates on a genome-wide level and at a single codon resolution.
source: Recently, our ability to measure translation rates was revolutionized by the technology of ribosome profiling, enabling the estimation of elongation rates on a genome-wide level and at a single codon resolution (Ingolia et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from Ingolia et al., 2009.

claim: The elongation rate can modulate protein folding and function.
source: Several studies indicate that the elongation rate can modulate protein folding and function (Kimchi-Sarfaty et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2009; Yona et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2013), but the underlying mechanisms are not yet well understood.
evidence: This is cited from multiple studies.

claim: Membrane proteins are extremely hydrophobic and aggregation-prone and are therefore inserted into the membrane co-translationally.
source: Membrane proteins are extremely hydrophobic and aggregation-prone and are therefore inserted into the membrane co-translationally (White and von Heijne, 2008; Luirink et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from White and von Heijne, 2008 and Luirink et al., 2012.

claim: Membrane proteins must be targeted to the translocon early in translation before large polypeptide portions are synthesized.
source: To do so, they must be targeted to the translocon early in translation before large polypeptide portions are synthesized (Lakkaraju et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from Lakkaraju et al., 2008.

claim: The SRP binds to the first transmembrane segment that emerges from the ribosome and directs it together with the translocon-associated SRP receptor to the translocon.
source: The pathway works such that the SRP binds to the first transmembrane segment (TM) that emerges from the ribosome and directs it together with the translocon-associated SRP receptor to the translocon.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the SRP pathway.

claim: The eukaryotic SRP arrests elongation to prevent protein synthesis before targeting is complete.
source: In eukaryotes, the SRP arrests the elongation upon binding to ribosome-nascent chain complexes, in order to prevent the protein synthesis before targeting is complete (Walter and Blobel, 1981; Mason et al., 2000).
evidence: This is cited from Walter and Blobel, 1981 and Mason et al., 2000.

claim: B. subtilis possesses the Alu domain of SRP RNA and this domain binds a protein (HBsu) that may function analogously to the eukaryotic SRP14.
source: Additionally, although SRP-mediated arrest was never demonstrated in B. subtilis, unlike E. coli, this organism may have all components required for SRP-mediated arrest: the Alu domain of SRP RNA is present and this domain binds a protein (HBsu) that may function analogously to the eukaryotic SRP14 (Nakamura et al., 1999).
evidence: This is cited from Nakamura et al., 1999.

claim: Unfolding or aggregation of GFP-fused proteins hinders GFP-folding and -fluorescence.
source: The discrimination is possible because unfolding or aggregation of fused proteins hinders GFP-folding and -fluorescence, whereas folded and fluorescent GFP is indicative of the functional and folded fused protein (Geertsma et al., 2008; Linares et al., 2010; Müller-Lucks et al., 2012; Schlegel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from multiple studies on the GFP-folding assay.

claim: Only the folded GFP-coupled forms of membrane proteins were soluble with mild detergent, while the unfolded forms were insoluble and probably aggregated.
source: The results of fractionation studies showed that only the folded GFP-coupled forms were soluble with mild detergent, while the unfolded forms were insoluble and probably aggregated (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A with experimental data.

claim: The cell's capacity to produce high amounts of folded membrane proteins is limited, and increased expression levels result in increased aggregation.
source: This indicates that regardless of the identity of the overexpressed protein, the cell's capacity to produce high amounts of folded membrane proteins is limited, and increased expression levels would result in increased aggregation.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation shown in Figure 5D.

claim: As total protein levels increase, the levels of folded proteins approach saturation.
source: Consistent with this notion, we observe that as total protein levels increase, the levels of folded proteins approach saturation (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Proteins that are translated fast saturated at relatively low amounts of folded protein, while slowly translated proteins converged to higher saturation levels.
source: However, the saturation curves show remarkable differences between proteins that are translated with different speed regimes in our codon range of interest. Proteins that are translated fast saturated at relatively low amounts of folded protein (apart from a single protein), while slowly translated proteins converged to higher saturation levels, if they saturated at all (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Slow translation during targeting supports less aggregation of the overexpressed proteins.
source: This effect is contributed by translation slowing at both codons 16 to 36 and at codons before TM2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A). The trend is also reflected by the difference between the groups in Figure 5D and suggests that slow translation during targeting supports less aggregation of the overexpressed proteins.
evidence: This is shown in Figures 5D and 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Slow translation is important especially at elevated protein amounts, when the cell's membrane protein biogenesis capacity might approach saturation.
source: Our results indicate that slow translation is important especially at elevated protein amounts, when the cell's membrane protein biogenesis capacity might approach saturation.
evidence: This is concluded from the expression experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: The arrest function in eukaryotes can be abolished by mutation without severely compromising viability.
source: In eukaryotes, the arrest function can be abolished by mutation without severely compromising viability (Mason et al., 2000; Lakkaraju et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from Mason et al., 2000 and Lakkaraju et al., 2008.

claim: Heterologous expression of eukaryotic membrane proteins in E. coli is notoriously difficult, often leading to poor expression of functional proteins.
source: Heterologous expression of eukaryotic membrane proteins in E. coli is notoriously difficult, often leading to poor expression of functional proteins, creating a serious bottleneck in the field (Granseth et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from Granseth et al., 2009.

claim: Gram-positive bacteria such as B. subtilis might be more compatible with eukaryotic membrane protein heterologous expression than E. coli.
source: It therefore seems that in that respect, Gram-positive bacteria such as B. subtilis might be more compatible with eukaryotic membrane protein heterologous expression (Kunji et al., 2005), since they contain a translation arrest logic similar to the eukaryotic one.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings and cited from Kunji et al., 2005.

claim: E. coli depends, at least in part, on a cis-encoded means to attenuate translation during targeting, presumably due to the lack of the Alu domain.
source: Remarkably, our results suggest that E. coli depends, at least in part, on a cis-encoded means to attenuate translation during targeting, presumably due to the lack of the Alu domain.
evidence: This is concluded from the analyses of E. coli and B. subtilis ribosome profiling data.

claim: The position of the pauses in E. coli is different from the position of Alu domain-mediated arrest, with the former occurring earlier in translation.
source: First, the position of the pauses in E. coli is different from the position of Alu domain-mediated arrest, with the former occurring earlier in translation.
evidence: This is observed from comparing E. coli and B. subtilis pause patterns.

claim: The prokaryotic pausing relies on information embedded in the mRNA, while the eukaryotic counterpart reads the protein.
source: Secondly, while the prokaryotic pausing relies on information embedded in the mRNA, the eukaryotic counterpart reads the protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the mechanisms described.

claim: The SRP-mediated arrest is only relieved after proper targeting and SRP-dissociation, thus ensuring the fidelity of the process.
source: The SRP-mediated arrest is only relieved after proper targeting and SRP-dissociation, thus ensuring the fidelity of the process (Akopian et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from Akopian et al., 2013.

claim: The mRNA-programmed mechanism probably pauses for a fixed amount of time, without any feedback about the targeting status.
source: In contrast, at present it is reasonable to guess that the mRNA-programmed mechanism probably pauses for a fixed amount of time, without any feedback about the targeting status.
evidence: This is speculated based on the nature of SD-mediated pauses.

claim: Both eukaryotes and prokaryotes possess limiting amounts of membrane protein biogenesis machineries, which may frequently be saturated, creating rate-limiting bottlenecks.
source: It therefore seems that both eukaryotes and prokaryotes possess limiting amounts of membrane protein biogenesis machineries, which may frequently be saturated, creating rate-limiting bottlenecks.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results and cited studies.

claim: Translation pauses are a general strategy that is employed when a process that requires only a portion of the polypeptide is hindered by additional polypeptide segments.
source: In a broader perspective, translation pauses are a general strategy that is employed when a process that requires only a portion of the polypeptide is hindered by additional polypeptide segments.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the study.

claim: Two processes that benefit from translation pauses are the co-translational targeting and the folding of individual domains in the multidomain proteins.
source: Two such processes are the co-translational targeting and the folding of individual domains in the multidomain proteins (Zhang et al., 2009; Pechmann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from Zhang et al., 2009 and Pechmann et al., 2013.

claim: SD-mediated pauses are probably lacking a priori in heterologous coding sequences expressed in E. coli.
source: For example, SD-mediated pauses are probably lacking a priori in heterologous coding sequences.
evidence: This is inferred from the findings about SD-mediated pauses.

claim: Codons constituting the 5% of the most dense codons genome-wide correspond to approximately sixfold higher density than the median density of genes in which they reside.
source: We considered 'pause codons' as those that constitute the 5% of the most dense codons genome-wide, corresponding to ∼sixfold higher density than the median density of genes in which they reside (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is the threshold used for pause calling as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Programmed pauses constitute approximately 2.5% of all codons.
source: Codons that passed both filters (high local density and SD-like element) constitute ∼2.5% of all codons and we refer to them as 'programmed pauses'.
evidence: This is calculated from the filtering criteria applied.

claim: The first and last four codons were excluded from pause analysis since they contain high density related to an initiation 'ramp' and translation termination.
source: The first and last four codons were excluded since they contain high density related to an initiation 'ramp' and translation termination, respectively (Tuller et al., 2010; Oh et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from Tuller et al., 2010 and Oh et al., 2011.

claim: Ribosome density in normalized profiles is inversely proportional to translation speed under steady-state conditions.
source: Assuming that ribosomes flow along mRNAs is in steady-state, ribosome density in these profiles is inversely proportional to translation speed (Tuller et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Tuller et al., 2010.

claim: The E. coli ribosome translates at a rate of 1 codon per 0.058 seconds.
source: To estimate translation time, we used a previously determined value of elongation rate for the E. coli ribosome of 1 codon per 0.058 s (Young and Bremer, 1976).
evidence: This is cited from Young and Bremer, 1976.

claim: Consecutive loops locations between the other TMs showed no significant enrichment for longer loop.
source: Consecutive loops locations between the other TMs showed no significant enrichment for longer loop (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Positively charged residues, glycine codons, or rare codons are not significantly enriched in codons 16-60 in membrane proteins.
source: In Figure 1—figure supplement 2, we exclude several such biases for membrane proteins, by showing that positively-charged residues, glycince codons, or rare codons are not significantly enriched in codons 16–60 in membrane proteins.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Periplasmic proteins show apparent depletion of pause in their N-terminal codons, likely due to the presence of N-terminal signal peptides.
source: Notably, however, such abundant biases in periplasmic proteins may explain the apparent depletion of pause in their N-terminal codons (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2), likely due to the presence of N-terminal signal peptides.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The main difference in amino acid composition before TM2 between proteins with intracellular vs extracellular N-termini is excess of arginines and lysines in proteins with extracellular N-termini.
source: To explore the difference between the two groups, we analyzed amino acid biases before TM2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A). The main difference was excess of arginines and lysines before the TM in proteins with extracellular N-termini, in accordance with the 'positive inside rule' (von Heijne, 2006).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and cited from von Heijne, 2006.

claim: The peak of pause before TM2 could not be explained by amino-acid biases at this location in proteins with intracellular N-termini.
source: Notably, when considering only the remaining proteins set (i.e., with intracellular N-termini), the peak of pause before TM2 could not be explained by amino-acid biases at this location since the slightly enriched amino acids there (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), are not encoded by G-nucleotide-rich codons that resemble the SD motif.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The peak of pause in membrane proteins was specifically related to TM2, as similar peaks were not found when aligning the coding sequences according to other TMs.
source: Furthermore, the peak of pause in the proteins was specifically related to TM2, as we could not find similar peaks when aligning the coding sequences according to other TMs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Slow elongation rates may rescue defects in the SRP-mediated targeting of membrane proteins with sub-optimal targeting signals.
source: This is consistent with a recent study showing that slow elongation rates may rescue defects in the SRP-mediated targeting of membrane proteins with sub-optimal targeting signals, likely by extending the time window for productive targeting (Zhang and Shan, 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Zhang and Shan, 2012.

claim: Slow translation at other more downstream codon locations may also be beneficial for folding.
source: Notably, slow translation at other more downstream codon locations may also be beneficial for folding (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Slow translation is much more common at codons 16-60 than downstream.
source: However, slow translation is much more common at codons 16–60, that is at the codon region that covers regions I and II, than downstream (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that slowing during targeting is of particular importance.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Regardless of the protein identity, slow translation during targeting is associated with better folding.
source: Overall, the results suggest that regardless of the protein identity, slow translation during targeting is associated with better folding.
evidence: This is concluded from the expression experiments.

claim: The effect of slow translation on folding appears to depend on expression level and is possibly required only when membrane protein biogenesis becomes saturated.
source: Yet, the effect appears to depend on expression level and is possibly required only when membrane protein biogenesis becomes saturated.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression level-dependent effects shown in Figure 5.

claim: The presence of pauses in many proteins may alleviate the burden on cellular quality control under endogenous expression levels.
source: We propose that the presence of pauses in many proteins may alleviate the burden on cellular quality control under endogenous expression levels.
evidence: This is proposed based on the findings.

claim: Notable pause peaks were observed when aligning B. subtilis coding sequences to TM2 and TM3, but these likely reflect shifted representations of the peak downstream to TM1.
source: Notable, albeit lower, pause peaks were also observed when aligning the coding sequences to TM2 and TM3 (Figure 7C). However, considering that the distance between TM1 and TM2 or TM3 is not very variable (median distances 35 and 72, respectively), these peaks most likely reflect shifted and skewed representations of the peak downstream to TM1.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C and explained by the analysis.

claim: The position of the pause 45-65 codons downstream to TM1 in B. subtilis agrees well with the exposure of the first TM out of the ribosome, where it can directly interact with the SRP.
source: The position of the pause 45–65 codons downstream to TM1 agrees well with the exposure of the first TM out of the ribosome, where it can directly interact with the SRP (Houben et al., 2005).
evidence: This is cited from Houben et al., 2005.

claim: The positioning of transmembrane segments along the sequence was comparable between E. coli and B. subtilis.
source: Notably, the positioning of transmembrane segments along the sequence was comparable between E. coli and B. subtilis (Figure 7A,B, orange bars and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A,B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.
